subject: Banking
title: AIG: The Insurance Company That Almost Killed Banking
description: One-minute skill: AIG: The Insurance Company That Almost Killed Banking.

hook.text: AIG sold $440 billion in credit default swaps — insurance on mortgage bonds.

buildup.text: Banks bought CDS from AIG to hedge their mortgage risk.

discovery.text: Those swaps looked like safe insurance until housing fell and AIG had to post collateral it did not have.

twist.text: Days after the bailout, AIG paid $165 million in executive bonuses.

climax.text: AIG proved that insurance companies can create systemic banking risk.

punchline.text: $440 billion in insurance. $185 billion bailout. Then executive bonuses.

quiz.question: What made AIG's failure so dangerous to the banking system?
options: Banks relied on AIG's credit default swaps as insurance against mortgage losses

details.summary: AIG sold hundreds of billions in credit default swaps guaranteeing bank assets without holding reserves to pay claims. When the housing market collapsed, AIG's inability to pay threatened to take down every major bank it had insured.
details.whyItMatters: AIG proved that a single non-bank institution could hold the entire financial system hostage. Its $182 billion government bailout remains the largest corporate rescue in history.
takeaways: AIG sold $440 billion in credit default swaps acting as insurance on bank assets
The $182 billion bailout was necessary to prevent cascading bank failures
AIG's Financial Products division operated with virtually no regulatory oversight

faq.question: How did an insurance company threaten the entire banking system?
faq.answer: AIG sold credit default swaps that guaranteed banks' mortgage-related assets. When those assets collapsed, AIG owed billions it could not pay. If AIG defaulted, every bank holding its guarantees would have faced massive uninsured losses simultaneously.

faq.question: Was AIG's bailout money ever repaid?
faq.answer: The US government eventually recovered its full $182 billion investment plus a $22.7 billion profit by selling its AIG stock holdings, making it one of the few profitable bailouts from the financial crisis.
